title: How Should a Christian Spend the Time They Have?
subtitle: You have a fixed number of days and you do not know the number. You spend them as though they were endless and resent them when they run short. Hurry has become the water you swim in, and the unexamined life keeps spilling out of you one rushed hour at a time. What it means to number your days, to read your calendar as a moral document, and to slow down enough to live the life you are actually living.

parts.title: The Year You Cannot Account For
parts.body:
Try to account for last Tuesday. Not the day in general, the actual hours. Where did they go. You were busy from waking to sleeping, you remember the fatigue clearly, and yet when you try to lay your hands on the day you find it has slipped between your fingers like water, an hour here on a screen you do not remember choosing, an hour there in a meeting that decided nothing, a thousand small interruptions that added up to a day and then a week and then a life you cannot quite locate. You are not lazy. You are busier than any generation in history. And you have the growing, uneasy sense that busy is not the same as alive.

The feeling has a particular texture at certain ages. The young parent who blinks and the baby is in kindergarten. The worker who looks up from the grind and a decade has passed. The person at fifty who realizes that the years are no longer arriving slowly, that time has begun to accelerate the way the bottom of a roll of tape spins faster as it empties, and who feels, under the productivity and the calendar invitations, a low dread that they are running out of something they never learned how to hold. You are spending the one resource you cannot earn more of, and you are spending it without examining the expense.

Underneath the busyness there is a quieter problem the busyness conveniently hides. You are not examining your life. Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living, and the church has its own sharper version, the unexamined Christian life, the faith carried along by momentum, never stopped, never weighed, never asked whether it is going anywhere. You do not examine your life because you are never still long enough to see it. The hurry is not only exhausting. It is a way of not looking, a noise loud enough to drown the questions you do not want to hear, and so the days pile up unexamined and the life you meant to live keeps getting postponed to a someday that the days are quietly using up.

Notice that you have made hurry a virtue. You answer how are you with the word busy and you say it almost proudly, as though a full calendar were the proof of a full life. You feel guilty when you are still. You check the phone in the line, at the light, in the bathroom, in the four seconds of silence that might otherwise have become a thought, because the silence has started to feel like a threat. You have lost the ability to do one thing at a time, to wait without reaching for distraction, to let a moment simply be a moment without harvesting it for something. You are, in the old and exact sense of the word, dissipated, your one life scattered across ten thousand fragments, none of them quite lived.

I built my own hurried life and then complained about it as though someone else had built it. I filled the calendar and resented the calendar. I let the phone eat the hours and called it staying connected. I told myself I had no time, which was a lie, because I had exactly as much time as everyone who ever lived, the same twenty-four hours given to Augustine and Bonhoeffer and my grandmother, and I was simply spending mine without looking at the receipt. The problem was never that I had too little time. The problem was that I had never learned to number my days.

parts.title: Hurry, the Great Enemy of the Soul
parts.body:
The spiritual director Dallas Willard was once asked by a busy pastor what he most needed to do to be healthy, and his answer has outlived him. You must ruthlessly eliminate hurry from your life, he said, for hurry is the great enemy of spiritual life today. He let it sit, then said it was the only thing on the list. Not laziness. Not even sin in the obvious sense. Hurry. Because hurry is not a schedule problem. It is a soul problem, and it quietly dismantles the very capacities the spiritual life requires, the capacity for attention, for presence, for love, for the slow and unhurried noticing of God and neighbor that no rushed person can manage.

Consider what hurry costs at the level of love, because love is the first casualty. Love takes time, unhurried time, the kind that cannot be optimized. The child does not need a more efficient parent. The child needs a present one, a parent slow enough to listen to a long boring story about a video game, and the hurried parent, even the one who loves the child fiercely, keeps missing the actual child while managing the child. The marriage does not die in a single betrayal. It dies in ten thousand rushed evenings where two people who love each other never quite stop moving long enough to be together. The Samaritan was not the busy one. The priest and the Levite were the busy ones, and they crossed to the other side of the road because they were on their way somewhere, and hurry made them, for that hour, incapable of the love their religion required. Hurry does not feel like sin. It feels like responsibility. And it leaves a trail of people you loved and never saw.

Consider too what hurry does to your relationship with God, which depends entirely on a kind of unhurried availability the rushed life cannot sustain. You cannot pray in a hurry, not really, not the prayer that listens. You cannot read Scripture for formation while skimming it for content between appointments. You cannot keep a Sabbath if every hour is spoken for, and you cannot wait on the Lord if you have lost the ability to wait for anything. The hurried Christian prays the way a man eats fast food in his car, getting the nutrition technically into the body while missing the entire point of the meal. God is not slow, but he is unhurried, and he keeps company with people at the pace of walking, not the pace of the freeway, and the rushed soul keeps showing up to the relationship out of breath and leaving before anything can happen.

And consider the final and largest cost, the unexamined life itself. The hurry is, at bottom, a flight from examination, and the flight has a destination you would not choose if you looked at it. You arrive at the end of a life you never quite inspected, having been busy the whole way, and you discover that busy was the means by which you avoided asking whether you were spending your days on what mattered. The watching skeptic sees this clearly, perhaps more clearly than the believer does. He sees Christians as hurried and scattered as everyone else, claiming a faith that promises peace while living at the same frantic pace as the people who claim nothing, and he reasonably concludes that the faith makes no difference to the one thing every human being is actually doing, which is spending a fixed and dwindling supply of days. An unhurried Christian would be a strange and arresting thing in this age. The rarity of it is its own indictment of us.

parts.title: Teach Us to Number Our Days
parts.body:
The Bible is not anxious about time and it is not casual about it. It holds time with a particular and bracing seriousness, beginning with the oldest psalm in the Psalter, the prayer of Moses in Psalm 90. The man of God looks at the brevity of human life against the eternity of God and does not flinch. A thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, he prays, and as a watch in the night. You sweep men away as with a flood. They are like grass, in the morning it flourishes and is renewed, in the evening it fades and withers. The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty, yet their span is but toil and trouble, they are soon gone, and we fly away. And out of that unsentimental reckoning with mortality comes the request that names the whole subject. So teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. The numbering is not morbid. It is the doorway to wisdom. The person who has truly faced the limit of his days is the only person free to spend them well.

Scripture returns to this again and again, refusing to let us pretend we have forever. James asks what is your life, and answers, you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. The Preacher in Ecclesiastes walks the reader straight to the grave to free him from wasting his life on what the wind will carry off. Paul tells the Ephesians to look carefully how they walk, making the best use of the time, redeeming it, because the days are evil. The word he uses is the language of the marketplace, buying back the time, treating each hour as a thing of value to be purchased deliberately rather than spent by default. The biblical posture toward time is neither the anxious hoarding of the productivity guru nor the careless drift of the procrastinator. It is the stewardship of a creature who knows the days are numbered, knows the number belongs to God, and means to spend each one as a trust.

And yet the same Scripture refuses to let the brevity of time become a frenzy. It commands rest as a holy discipline. Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, but the seventh is a Sabbath to the Lord. The God who made time built a stopping into it, a weekly refusal to treat the hours as nothing but raw material for output, a regular declaration that the world will go on turning while you rest, because you are not the one holding it together. The Sabbath is a frontal assault on hurry, a structural insistence that there is a limit to your labor and that the limit is good, that you are a creature and not a machine, and that the proof of your trust in God is your willingness to stop. A people who cannot stop do not believe, whatever they say, that the world is held by anyone but themselves.

Jesus himself, who had the shortest possible window to accomplish the most important work in history, was never in a hurry. Read the Gospels for pace and it astonishes you. He had three years to save the world and he spent them walking, stopping, eating long meals, sleeping through storms, withdrawing to lonely places to pray while crowds waited, refusing to be rushed even by the death of his friend Lazarus, even by the urgency of the sick pressing in. When the woman with the hemorrhage touched his garment in the middle of a crowd on the way to a dying child, he stopped, in the press and the urgency, to find her and to speak with her, unhurried in the one moment that most demanded haste. He was the most purposeful person who ever lived and the least frantic, and the combination is the whole lesson. Purpose does not require hurry. Hurry is usually purpose's enemy.

Underneath all of it lies the deepest truth Scripture tells about time, that it belongs to God and is held by God. My times are in your hand, prays David, and the line dissolves the anxiety at its root. Your days are not a resource you must frantically protect because there is no one else minding them. They are held by a Father who knows the number, who has appointed your times and the boundaries of your dwelling, who is not pacing nervously over the clock. This is why the believer can be both serious and unhurried about time, can number his days without dread and spend them without panic, because the One who gave the days is keeping them, and the same hand that holds the world holds the calendar. To live as though time were yours to hoard or yours to waste is, in either direction, to forget whose it is.

parts.title: Augustine, the Monastery, and the Long Discipline of Time
parts.body:
No one in the Christian tradition has thought harder about time than Augustine of Hippo, who in the eleventh book of his Confessions, written around the year 397, stops his life story to ask the question that had haunted him. What then is time. If no one asks me, I know, he writes, but if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I know not. He wrestles with the strange truth that the past is no longer, the future is not yet, and the present has no duration, that time seems to exist only in the soul that holds the no-longer in memory, attends to the fleeting now, and reaches toward the not-yet in expectation. And out of that famous difficulty he draws a spiritual diagnosis that names our condition exactly. The fallen soul, he says, is distended, stretched out and scattered across time, dissipated among the many, pulled apart by the rush of things passing. The remedy is to be gathered and collected back into one by reaching toward the eternal God who is not scattered across moments but holds all things in an eternal present. Augustine saw, sixteen hundred years before the smartphone, that the disease of the restless soul is fragmentation across time, and that the cure is to be recollected in God.

The monastic tradition built an entire civilization of time around exactly that insight. When Benedict wrote his Rule in the sixth century, he ordered the whole day by the bells, the hours of prayer marking the morning, the midday, the evening, and the night, so that time itself was sanctified and structured rather than left to drift. The monks rose, prayed, worked, ate, and slept by a rhythm that refused both the frenzy of overwork and the sloth of disorder, and they held idleness to be an enemy of the soul precisely because they took time so seriously as a gift to be stewarded. The medieval monastery was, among other things, a school for the redemption of time, a place that proved a human community could live by rhythms of unhurried attention rather than the tyranny of the urgent. The very clocks that would later mechanize the modern world were first built in monasteries, to ring the hours of prayer, a fact heavy with irony, since the instrument invented to order time toward God would be turned by a later age into the master that orders human beings toward output.

That later turn is one of the great hidden stories of the modern world, and the historian E. P. Thompson traced it with care. Before the industrial revolution, human beings lived largely by task time, working until the task was done and resting when it was, by the rhythms of the sun, the seasons, and the bell. The factory and the clock changed everything. Time became money, abstract, measurable, divisible into units to be bought and sold, and the worker learned to live by the clock on the wall rather than the rhythm of the work or the body. The philosopher Josef Pieper, writing in the rubble of postwar Germany in his book Leisure, the Basis of Culture, saw what this had cost. He argued that a civilization given over entirely to total work, to the worship of usefulness and output, loses the capacity for leisure in the deep sense, the contemplative stillness in which a human being beholds reality and worships God, and that without it culture itself withers, because culture is born in leisure, not in labor. The modern person, Pieper warned, no longer knows how to be still, and has forgotten that the highest human activities, prayer, contemplation, festivity, the love of God, cannot be hurried and cannot be turned into work.

The Sabbath tradition kept the resistance alive across the centuries. The Jewish theologian Abraham Joshua Heschel wrote in 1951 a small book called The Sabbath that named the stakes more beautifully than anyone. The Sabbath, he said, is a cathedral in time, not in space, a sanctuary that we build not out of stone but out of hours, a palace in time into which we withdraw one day in seven to remember that we are not slaves and that the world is held by God. Heschel saw modern people as exiles in time, frantic conquerors of space who had lost the art of dwelling in the hour, and he held up the Sabbath as the great correction, a weekly declaration of independence from the tyranny of the urgent. The Puritans before him had taken the Lord's day with the same seriousness, ordering their week around it, and Eugene Peterson in our own time recovered the unhurried pastoral life against a church that had grown as frantic and program-driven as the corporations it imitated. Peterson insisted that the pastor, of all people, must not be busy, must refuse the hurry that makes attention to God and souls impossible, must keep a Sabbath and a slow morning and the long unhurried work of being present, because a hurried shepherd cannot tend a flock and a hurried soul cannot love. The whole tradition, monk and Puritan and pastor and rabbi, has been saying one thing across the centuries. Time is holy, time is short, time is God's, and the unhurried life is not a luxury but the only soil in which a soul can grow.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The believer who takes time seriously is free to learn from anyone who has studied how human beings actually spend their hours, while testing each account against the God in whose hand our times rest. The thinkers below have each seen something true about time, attention, and the finite life, and each must be measured against Scripture, because every account of how to spend our days carries a hidden answer to the question of whose days they are.

secular.author: Oliver Burkeman
secular.whatItGetsRight: Burkeman takes the average human lifespan, about four thousand weeks, and uses the brutal smallness of the number to demolish the fantasy of the productivity culture, the lie that with better systems you could finally get on top of your time and do everything. You cannot. You are finite, the to-do list is infinite, and the only sane path is to accept your limits, choose what you will neglect, and actually live the few weeks you have rather than endlessly optimizing toward a control you will never reach. This is Psalm 90 translated for the productivity age, the numbering of days as the doorway to wisdom.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Burkeman counts the weeks honestly and finds no one holding them. His finitude is a closed system, a brief flicker between two oblivions, and his counsel is finally a noble Stoic resignation, make peace with death because there is nothing on the other side of it. Psalm 90 numbers the same days and prays to the eternal God who has been our dwelling place in all generations, so that the brevity drives not to resignation but to wisdom held in trust. Burkeman can free you from the productivity lie and cannot give you the dwelling place. The believer numbers his days knowing they are held by a Father, and so the smallness of the number becomes not a wall but a gift, four thousand weeks placed in a hand that will not drop them.

secular.source: Stolen Focus and the attention economy
secular.author: Johann Hari
secular.whatItGetsRight: Hari documents how an entire industry has been engineered to capture and fragment human attention for profit, how the rush and the scatter we feel are not personal failures but the designed product of systems that make money from our distraction. He shows that the inability to be still, to read deeply, to do one thing at a time, has been manufactured, and that reclaiming attention is partly a matter of resisting machines built to steal it. This confirms from the side of investigation what the contemplative tradition knew, that a scattered attention is a diminished soul.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Hari names the external thief and underweights the internal one. Scripture agrees that the age conspires to scatter us, the days are evil, redeem the time, but it knows the deeper restlessness is in the heart, not only in the phone, that even a person stranded on a desert island with no device would find his attention scattered by a soul not yet recollected in God. Augustine saw that the distention of the soul across time is a spiritual condition, healed not merely by deleting an app but by being gathered back into one through the love of the eternal God. Hari can help you fight the thief at the door. Only grace addresses the dissipation that was already inside the house.

secular.source: Deep Work and the economics of attention
secular.author: Cal Newport
secular.whatItGetsRight: Newport argues that the ability to focus without distraction on a cognitively demanding task is both increasingly rare and increasingly valuable, and that the constant shallow busyness of the modern worker, the email and the meetings and the notifications, destroys the capacity for the concentrated work that actually matters. He recovers, in secular and practical terms, the lost art of doing one thing at a time with the whole of one's attention, and shows that the unhurried, focused life is not only spiritually richer but more effective.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Newport recovers focus and aims it at productivity, at building a valuable career and a meaningful working life. Scripture honors the focused life and reorders its end, because the goal of redeeming the time is not finally a more valuable you but a life spent for God and neighbor. Deep work in the service of self is still a sophisticated form of the total work Pieper warned against, attention gathered for output rather than for worship and love. The believer wants the focus Newport teaches and wants it bent toward the unhurried attention to God, to the child, to the stranger, that no career metric can measure. The discipline is borrowed gladly. The end is corrected entirely.

secular.source: Sabbath and the limits of the human machine
secular.author: Wayne Muller
secular.whatItGetsRight: Muller writes movingly about how the loss of Sabbath, of any regular and protected stopping, has left modern people exhausted and depleted, treating themselves as machines that should run without rest. He recovers the wisdom that rest is not earned by finishing the work, because the work is never finished, but is a discipline practiced in the middle of the unfinished, a deliberate ceasing that restores the soul and the body and reminds us that we are not the ones holding the world together.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Muller draws on the Sabbath broadly, as one wisdom tradition among many, and loosens it from its anchor. The biblical Sabbath is not a self-care technique for the depleted but a covenant sign, rooted in the God who rested on the seventh day and in the redemption from slavery in Egypt, a worship before it is a rest. Remember the Sabbath to keep it holy, holy to the Lord, not merely restorative to you. Muller can return rest to the exhausted, and Scripture deepens it from therapy into worship, from a strategy for sustainability into a weekly confession that the world is held by God and not by your labor. The rest is real either way. Only in Scripture is it also an act of trust.

secular.author: the mindfulness and meditation movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: The wide modern turn to mindfulness and meditation has rediscovered, often outside any religious frame, that human beings are starving for stillness, that the unexamined and unattended life is impoverished, and that the simple practice of slowing down, breathing, and being present to the moment has measurable effects on a frazzled mind. It is a real witness, drawn largely from contemplative traditions, that the hurried life is a sickness and that stillness is medicine.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The movement teaches stillness and largely empties it of the One the stillness is for. Its goal is often a calm and centered self, attention turned inward to the breath and the present moment with no Other on the far side of the silence. The biblical word is be still, and know that I am God, and the knowing is the whole point. Christian stillness is not the emptying of the mind but the filling of it with attention to a Person, not presence to the moment but presence to the God who holds the moment. Mindfulness can quiet the frantic mind and cannot tell it who is in the room. Scripture leads the same restless soul into a silence that turns out to be full, the unhurried company of the God in whose hand our times are held.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who agree that time is holy and hurry is a danger still differ over how rigidly to structure the redemption of time, and especially over how to keep the Sabbath in a world that has forgotten how. The question is whether faithfulness in time is mainly a matter of disciplined structure or mainly a matter of inner freedom and rhythm. Hear each at its strongest, because both are guarding a real treasure against a real loss.

views.view: Guard time with disciplined structure and a kept Sabbath
views.body: This view holds that in an age engineered to steal your hours, only a deliberate and somewhat rigid structure will protect what matters, and that the Sabbath in particular must be kept as a real and protected boundary, not a vague intention. Advocates point to the fourth commandment standing in the Decalogue alongside the prohibitions of murder and theft, weighty, concrete, and binding, and they argue that a day genuinely set apart, with real limits on work and screens and commerce, is not legalism but love, a structure that secures the rest the soul cannot achieve by good intentions alone. They look at the monastic hours and the Puritan Lord's day and see the wisdom of a people who knew that the heart will not protect its own time and must be helped by a rule. They warn that the modern preference for flexibility and rhythm over structure tends, in practice, to dissolve into no boundary at all, until the Sabbath becomes a feeling that never quite arrives and the hours leak away exactly as the age intends. The danger they are guarding against is real, a frictionless life with no protected time at all, a faith that talks about rest while living at the same frantic pace as the world, a soul scattered for lack of any wall to hold it. Against that they hold that you must build the structure, keep the day, draw the boundary, and trust that the discipline is not a cage but a trellis on which an unhurried life can finally grow. They concede the danger of their own position, a structure that hardens into mere rule-keeping and forgets the rest is for the soul and not the soul for the rest, and they insist the answer is not to abandon the structure but to keep filling it with its purpose.

views.view: Hold time with inner freedom and life-giving rhythm
views.body: This view holds that the redemption of time is finally a matter of the heart and its rhythms rather than a rigid schedule, and it points to the way Jesus and Paul treated the Sabbath with a striking freedom. The Lord declared himself lord of the Sabbath, healed on it, let his disciples pluck grain on it, and insisted the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath. Paul told the Romans not to let anyone pass judgment on them regarding a festival or a Sabbath, that one person esteems one day above another while another esteems all days alike, and that each should be fully convinced in his own mind. Advocates argue that the New Testament loosens the rigid letter precisely so the deeper rest can be received as gift rather than performed as law, and that the unhurried life is grown by cultivating life-giving rhythms of work and rest, prayer and presence, suited to one's actual life, rather than by imposing a one-size structure that becomes its own kind of bondage. The danger they are guarding against is real, a Sabbath-keeping that hardens into the very legalism Jesus rebuked, a structure so rigid it crushes the people it was meant to free, a soul keeping the day perfectly and missing the rest entirely. Against that they hold that the goal is a heart at rest in God, an unhurried availability that flows from trust rather than from a rule, and that the rhythms which serve that rest will look different in different lives and seasons. They concede, in turn, the danger of their own position, that freedom without structure tends to evaporate into no rest at all, and they insist that genuine inner freedom will build real rhythms and real limits, not use grace as an excuse for the same old hurry.

parts.title: What the Examined Life Forms in a Person
parts.body:
Numbering your days is not an idea you adopt but a slow re-education of the whole self, and the unhurried, examined life is grown rather than decided. You cannot become an unhurried person by hurrying to become one. You are formed into it gradually, by practice and by grace, as the frantic patterns of years are unlearned and something steadier takes their place, and along the way God forms specific things in the one who stops to look.

He forms presence, the simple and increasingly rare capacity to actually be where you are. The hurried person is never present, always slightly ahead of himself, attending the meeting while planning the next one, sitting with the child while checking the phone, living perpetually in a future that swallows the only moment he was ever given, the present one. The person being formed by the examined life slowly comes back into the present, learns to do one thing at a time, to listen to the end of the sentence, to taste the meal, to be with the person in front of him rather than managing them on the way to somewhere else. This presence is the soil of all love, and the hurried cannot grow it, and the unhurried can hardly help it.

He forms the wisdom that comes only from examination. The unexamined life rushes past its own lessons, repeats its own mistakes, never stops long enough to ask what the last decade was teaching, and so accumulates years without accumulating wisdom. The person who has learned to stop and number his days develops a reflective capacity the busy life forbids, the ability to read his own experience, to see the patterns, to catch the slow drift before it becomes a destiny, to course-correct while there is still time to correct. This is the heart of wisdom Psalm 90 promises to the one who numbers his days, and it does not come to those who never stop running long enough to look back.

He forms a right relationship with mortality, which is the strangest gift of all. Most people manage their fear of death by never looking at it, staying busy enough to avoid the thought, and the avoidance quietly poisons everything, because a life organized around not noticing it will end is a life that cannot fully begin. The person who has learned to number his days has looked at the limit and made a kind of peace with it, not a morbid obsession but a clear-eyed acceptance that frees rather than frightens. He is, paradoxically, the most awake person in the room, more alive precisely because he has stopped pretending he has forever, able to receive each ordinary day as the gift it is rather than the endless supply he assumed. The Christian faces death not as a void but as a doorway, and the one who has numbered his days in that hope lives with an unhurried freedom the death-denying world can never reach.

And he forms trust, the deepest formation of all, the trust that lets a finite creature stop trying to hold infinite time. The frenzy is, at bottom, a failure of faith, the frantic effort of a soul that does not really believe anyone else is minding the clock, that thinks it must squeeze and hoard and optimize because the days are slipping and no one is keeping them. The person being formed learns to pray my times are in your hand and to mean it, and the meaning loosens the grip, lets him work hard without panic and rest without guilt, spend his days deliberately without the dread that he is wasting a resource no one is replenishing. He has not stopped taking time seriously. He has stopped taking it anxiously, because he has come to believe that the same hand that gave the days is keeping them, and that the One who holds the world is more than capable of holding the calendar. That trust is the end of hurry, and it is the beginning of being, at last, unhurried and alive.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: You will not slow down by resolving to slow down. Hurry is unlearned the way it was learned, gradually, by practice, by building actual limits and rhythms into a life that has none. None of what follows will make you unhurried by next week. All of it will start to loosen the grip of the clock if you keep at it. Begin with the one practice that most frightens you, which is usually the one you most need, and let the rest follow as the pace changes.

steps: Account for one full day, hour by hour, written down honestly. Where did the time actually go. Not where you meant it to go, where it went. The audit is the beginning of the examined life, and most people have never once looked at the receipt for a single day.

Pray Psalm 90 slowly, out loud, once. Teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. Let the prayer of Moses do its work on your sense of the brevity and the value of the time you have left.

Drive once, or walk once, or wait in one line, with no phone and no podcast, in silence, and do not reach for distraction. Notice how hard it is. The difficulty is the diagnosis. The silence you cannot tolerate is exactly the silence your soul most needs.

Do one ordinary thing this week with your whole attention, one meal, one conversation, one task, at the pace it actually requires, refusing to rush it or to do anything else at the same time. Practice presence once, on purpose, and notice what it gives back.

Keep one real Sabbath, a genuine day with actual limits on work and screens and errands, a protected cathedral of hours into which you withdraw to rest, worship, and remember that the world will keep turning without your labor. Do not perfect it. Keep it.

Examine your calendar as a moral document, because it is one. Your calendar, not your stated values, reveals what you actually worship, where your time and therefore your love truly go. Read it honestly and let the gap between what you say matters and what your hours show convict you.

Identify the one hurry that costs you the most love, the rushing past a particular person, and deliberately slow down for them this month. Give one person the unhurried presence they have been missing, and watch what the slowing does to the bond.

Build one small structural limit on the thief of your attention. A phone that sleeps in another room. A fixed hour with no screen. A morning that begins in stillness before it begins in input. One wall against the machines built to scatter you.

Establish a daily rhythm of unhurried attention to God, a fixed and protected time, however short, that does not get eaten by the urgent. Read Scripture for formation, not information, slowly enough to be changed. Pray at the pace of listening, not the pace of the freeway.

Read Augustine on time, the eleventh book of the Confessions, and let his ancient diagnosis name your modern condition, the soul distended and scattered across moments, in need of being gathered back into one through the love of the eternal God.

Conduct a regular examination of your life, weekly or monthly, in which you actually stop and look. Where am I going. Is it where I mean to go. What is the last season teaching me. What needs to change while there is still time to change it. The unexamined Christian life ends in regret it never saw coming.

Prune the calendar deliberately, since you cannot do everything and the attempt is destroying you. Choose what you will neglect, on purpose, in the light of what actually matters, and let the no to the lesser things be the form your yes to the greater things takes.

Make the Sabbath a settled architecture of your year, a kept rhythm that shapes your whole life rather than an occasional good intention, until the weekly stopping has become the trellis on which an unhurried existence has grown, your standing weekly confession that the world is held by God and not by you.

Aim, over years, at becoming an unhurried person, which is different from a less busy one. Let the frantic patterns of a lifetime be slowly unlearned until presence, attention, and a steady pace have become simply who you are, a strange and arresting witness in a frantic age.

Make peace with your own mortality in the hope of the resurrection, returning each year to the numbering of your days, until the limit no longer frightens you but frees you, and you receive each ordinary day as the gift it is rather than the endless supply you once assumed.

Keep praying my times are in your hand until the grip loosens for good, until you can work without panic and rest without guilt because you have come to believe, all the way down, that the same hand which gave you the days is keeping them, and that you were never the one holding the clock.
